Subject: Clarify: stepwise credits vs effective rate example

Hi Laura —

Thanks for the call this morning. The procurement team asked for a concrete worked example so they can compare the per-token ladder vs a blended effective rate across our forecasted volumes. They want to understand:

- How credits/accelerators apply at each breakpoint (are they one-time offsets or recurring until true-up?)
- Whether we show marginal pricing math or just the blended effective $/1K tokens for the total committed volume
- An example showing real numbers using our Q1-Q4 forecast attached to this thread (I attached a cleaned extract to the spreadsheet).

Can you send a short worked example with both marginal and blended calculations and a recommendation for which structure reduces complexity for procurement but preserves Redwood's economics? Procurement would like to see the model before the Friday executive procurement review.

Appreciate it —
Ellen Park
Head of Platform Procurement, SentryCloud
procurement@sentrycloud.com

Attachment(s): sentry_forecast_q1q4.csv

From: laura_bennett <laura_bennett@redwood.ai>
To: Ellen Park <ellen.park@sentrycloud.com>
Cc: aditya_rao@redwood.ai, dev_patel@redwood.ai
Date: Wed, 1 Dec 2027 12:45:00 -08:00
Subject: Re: Clarify: stepwise credits vs effective rate example

Ellen —

Thanks for the clear ask and the forecast. Attached is a short worked example (sheet: 'WorkedExample') that lays out both approaches and the effective $/1K tokens so you can drop it into procurement's comparison tool. Two quick clarifications before you show it to legal/procurement:

1) Credits vs. recurring offsets: our proposed "accelerator credits" are applied monthly against that month’s invoice once the monthly token consumption crosses a breakpoint; they are not one-time refunds. At year true-up we reconcile any over/under consumption against committed annual volume (standard true-up).

2) Marginal vs blended: the marginal view shows the per-token price that applies within each band (useful for understanding marginal economics). The blended view shows the single effective $/1K tokens if you divide total spend by total tokens across the committed period — easier for procurement to compare against a competitor flat blended quote.

Summary (numbers in the attachment):
- Forecast total tokens (annual): 9,600,000k tokens (9.6B tokens)
- Example breakpoints: 0-1,000k @ $0.030/1K; next 4,000k @ $0.020/1K; above 5,000k @ $0.012/1K (marginal).
- Marginal spend = sum(band_tokens * band_rate) = $... (see sheet).
- Blended effective = total_spend / total_tokens = $0.0148/1K (example result).

Recommendation: present both. Procurement will like the blended number for simple comparisons; finance and engineering care about marginal for forecasting handing of burst costs. We typically include both on the SOW with a brief note: "Rates charged on a marginal basis; blended effective rate shown for comparison and invoicing transparency."

I'm looping in Aditya on the exact wording for the SOW and Dev for any upper-bound caps we should include. If procurement wants a simpler single-line item, we can produce a single blended fixed effective-rate offer in exchange for a +15% commit uplift.

Regards,
Laura Bennett
Senior Account Executive, Redwood Inference
laura_bennett@redwood.ai
(Attachment: sentry_pricing_model_v3.xlsx)

From: aditya_rao <aditya_rao@redwood.ai>
To: laura_bennett <laura_bennett@redwood.ai>, dev_patel@redwood.ai
Date: Wed, 1 Dec 2027 15:10:00 -08:00
Subject: Fwd: Clarify: stepwise credits vs effective rate example

LAURA / DEV —

I pulled the math into the model and added a simple marginal vs blended comparison table on tab 'ComparisonSummary'. Key points to flag to SentryCloud procurement:

- With the breakpoints Laura proposed, the marginal schedule preserves unit economics at scale (we do not lose margin on the top band because only the incremental tokens get the lower price).
- The blended number looks attractive (~$0.0148/1K in the example) but hides that initial band is materially higher — if they have heavy burst months below the breakpoint profile, their month-to-month invoices could be higher than the blended implies.
- If SentryCloud requests a single-line blended invoice, we should include an explicit contract clause that defines the billing method (monthly invoiced as blended vs marginal) and a true-up mechanism at the end of the year. 

I also added a short sensitivity table that shows what happens to effective $/1K if they under-deliver by 20% (blended moves up ~18%) — good figure for procurement negotiation.

One operational ask: Dev, can you confirm whether we can implement a monthly cap protection (soft cap) that prevents invoices exceeding X% above forecast in any given month? If yes, we can trade that cap for a tighter blended rate.

- Aditya

From: dev_patel <dev_patel@redwood.ai>

Date: Thu, 2 Dec 2027 11:05:00 -08:00
Subject: Re: Clarify: stepwise credits vs effective rate example

Ellen / Laura / Aditya —

Quick operational confirmation from infra side: we can support a soft monthly cap that smooths spikes for billing purposes. Implementation details:

- Soft cap is configurable per-customer; for SentryCloud I recommend a 40% monthly spike cap relative to their monthly committed baseline (we can tune).
- If usage exceeds the soft cap, tokens above the cap will be throttled by request queueing for non-critical traffic; critical routes can opt-out but will be billed at the higher marginal band.
- Soft cap option requires us to add a short clause to the SOW for provisioning and emergency unthrottling (10 business days SLA for change).

I'll ask product to add the soft cap toggle to the onboarding checklist for Dedicated/Hosted customers; legal should get a brief SOW paragraph.

Ellen — if that sounds ok I'll ask Contracts to draft the SOW using the marginal billing model with optional blended fixed-rate in exchange for +15% commit, and include the soft cap clause.

Thanks,
Dev Patel
Director, Platform Operations — Redwood Inference
